name: God's Own Junkyard
description: A Walthamstow warehouse of vintage and custom neon signs — a third-generation sign-maker's chaotic paradise of glowing neon art.
address: Unit 12, Ravenswood Industrial Estate, London E17 9HQ
tips: Open Fri-Sun only. The Rolling Scones Café inside serves tea and cake.

name: The Last Tuesday Society (Viktor Wynd Museum)
description: A tiny Hackney museum of curiosities — taxidermy, occult oddities, and a cocktail bar downstairs. The weirdest collection in London.
tips: Combined museum-plus-cocktail tickets available. Tuesday nights feature taxidermy workshops.

name: Crossness Pumping Station
description: The 'Cathedral on the Marsh' — Bazalgette's 1865 sewage pumping station, astonishing painted Victorian ironwork in Abbey Wood.
tips: Steaming days are special — book ahead. Abbey Wood Elizabeth Line station.

name: Leake Street Graffiti Tunnel
description: A 300-metre tunnel beneath Waterloo Station — London's only legal graffiti wall, endlessly repainted by street artists.
tips: Street-food vendors and bars inside the arches. Artists often at work on Saturdays.

name: Crystal Palace Subway
description: A vaulted polychrome-brick subway (1865) that once led from the old railway station to the Crystal Palace. A surviving Victorian secret.
tips: Open select heritage days only — including Open House London.

name: Severndroog Castle
description: A Gothic triangular folly (1784) on top of Shooter's Hill — 7 counties visible from the roof on a clear day.
tips: Open first Sunday of the month and heritage days. Woolwich is nearest station.

name: St Dunstan in the East
description: A bombed-out Wren church turned public garden — ivy-drenched ruins, fountains, a hidden green cathedral in the City.
tips: Free. Quiet on weekends. Photogenic in any season.

name: Pickering Place
description: London's smallest public square, tucked behind Berry Bros & Rudd off St James's Street — gas-lit, Georgian, and once Texas's London embassy.
tips: Access through the narrow passage beside Berry Bros & Rudd wine merchants.

name: Goodwin's Court
description: A Dickensian alley of 17th-century bow-fronted shops — unchanged since before 1700, gas-lit at night.
tips: Best photographed at dusk when the gas lamps come on.

name: Brydges Place
description: The narrowest alley in London — 15 inches wide at its slenderest, beside the Coliseum.
tips: You may need to go sideways.

name: Crosby Square Banksy
description: An original Banksy 'maid sweeping under the wall' in a City side street — one of the few Banksy works still visible in central London.
tips: Street art moves — check current locations online before visiting.

name: Red Phone Box Row
description: Broad Court in Covent Garden — a rare surviving row of four K2 red phone boxes, the iconic Giles Gilbert Scott design.
tips: Opposite the Royal Opera House stage door — often spotted by dancers.

name: The Cabmen's Shelter Kensington
description: One of 13 surviving green wooden cabmen's shelters (1875) — refreshment-stops for London's taxi drivers since Queen Victoria's reign.
tips: For use by licensed cabbies only — but you can admire from outside.

name: Green Parakeet Spotting, Kensington Gardens
description: Thousands of bright-green ring-necked parakeets have colonised London's parks — Kensington Gardens is the best spotting ground.
tips: Bring apples or seeds — they'll land on your hand.

name: Coal Tax Posts
description: Ring of cast-iron posts (1860s) marking the boundary where 19th-century London charged a tax on coal — 210 survive, most hidden.
tips: Check the 'Coal Tax Posts' website for the current locations.

name: The Seven Noses of Soho
description: Seven plaster noses attached to Soho walls by artist Rick Buckley in 1997 as protest against CCTV — find all seven and gain wealth (supposedly).
tips: Treasure-hunt clues on 'Secret London' blog.

name: Cleopatra's Needle
description: A 3,500-year-old Egyptian obelisk on Victoria Embankment — older than London itself. Time capsule sealed at base.
tips: Look for the WWI shrapnel scars on the nearby sphinxes.

name: Walkie Talkie Scorch Mark
description: 20 Fenchurch Street's (The Walkie Talkie's) concave glass famously melted a parked Jaguar in 2013 — a discreet plaque remembers the event.
tips: Sunscreens were added to fix the death-ray effect.

name: London Mithraeum
description: A 3rd-century Roman temple dramatically reinstalled beneath Bloomberg's HQ — sound, mist, and period-accurate lighting.
tips: Free but book ahead — timed entry. Allow time for the contemporary art exhibition upstairs.

name: London Stone
description: A piece of limestone behind a decorative grille on Cannon Street — possibly a Roman milestone, certainly London's oldest urban relic.
tips: Visible 24 hours through the grille. Shakespeare mentioned it in Henry VI.

name: Roman Bath Strand Lane
description: A 'Roman' bath (actually 17th-century) beneath Surrey Street — National Trust, visible through a window only.
tips: Opens rarely — check National Trust website. Mentioned in Dickens's 'David Copperfield'.

name: Roman City Wall at Tower Hill
description: A 20m section of 2nd-century Roman wall in Cooper's Row — the tallest surviving fragment of Londinium's defences.
tips: Free, public, 24/7. Best seen in natural light.

name: St Ethelburga's Centre
description: A tiny Bishopsgate church (14th century) survived the Great Fire and Blitz before the 1993 IRA bomb — rebuilt as a peace centre.
tips: Free. Tuesday-Thursday 12-4pm. Garden tent out back.

name: St Olave Hart Street
description: 'The church that Dickens called 'St Ghastly Grim' — survived the Great Fire, has Samuel Pepys buried inside, skulls on the gate.
tips: Free. Don't miss Pepys's memorial to his wife inside.

name: Watts Memorial, Postman's Park
description: GF Watts's 1900 memorial wall of hand-painted tiles — each tile commemorates an ordinary Victorian Londoner who died saving another.
tips: Read every tile — each is a story. The park is a named 'Magnificent Seven' hidden garden.

name: Dennis Severs' House
description: Ten rooms frozen in time — artist Dennis Severs recreated 200 years of an imaginary Huguenot family's life, room by room. Silent tour only.
tips: Silent tour only. No phones. Candle-lit evenings (£20) are magical.

name: 18 Stafford Terrace (Sambourne House)
description: Victorian illustrator Linley Sambourne's house preserved virtually untouched since 1874 — a perfect Aesthetic Movement time capsule.
tips: Wednesday-Sunday. Timed entry.

name: The Charterhouse
description: A medieval monastery turned Tudor mansion turned almshouse — still housing 40 'brothers', open for small guided tours only.
tips: Guided tour only — book weeks ahead. Chapel free to visit.

name: Two Temple Place
description: A late-Victorian Neo-Gothic mansion built for William Waldorf Astor — free exhibitions each year, extraordinary panelled interiors.
tips: Only open Jan-April when hosting exhibitions. Free entry.

name: Leighton House Museum
description: Victorian painter Frederic Leighton's fantasy Islamic-palace home — a gold-domed Arab Hall tiled with Damascene ceramics.
tips: Arab Hall is the show-stopper. Closed Tuesdays.

name: Dennis Severs' Silent Night
description: Evening candle-lit tour of Dennis Severs' House — 45 minutes of near-total silence as you move through the 10 period rooms.
tips: Tickets Mondays/Wednesdays. Silence strictly enforced.

name: Postal Museum Mail Rail
description: The underground Post Office Railway (1927) — a 100-year-old narrow-gauge line 20m beneath Mount Pleasant. Ride the trains.
tips: Book Mail Rail tickets ahead. Entry includes the museum above.

name: Hidden London Underground Tours
description: TfL's official access to disused Tube stations — Aldwych, Down Street, Moorgate. Wartime Churchill bunkers and ghost platforms.
tips: Book 3 months ahead — sell out within an hour.

name: Brunel Museum & Thames Tunnel
description: Marc Brunel's 1843 Thames Tunnel — the world's first under-water tunnel — with the original shaft now a museum and occasional underground venue.
tips: Rotherhithe Overground. Shaft concerts and tours monthly.

name: Wapping Hydraulic Power Station
description: A Victorian hydraulic power station (1890) — once powered London's lifts, now a Frank Bruno restaurant (occasionally open).
tips: Exterior visible anytime. Occasionally open for events.

name: London Watermill
description: Morden Hall Park's working 19th-century snuff mill — one of London's last surviving water-powered mills.
tips: National Trust. Free entry.

name: Camley Street Natural Park
description: A 2-acre wildlife reserve beside King's Cross Station — urban wilderness on a former coal yard with a pond, visitor centre, and rare plants.
tips: London Wildlife Trust. Community-built. Free.

name: Phoenix Garden
description: A secret WW2 bombsite-turned-community-garden in Soho — pond, benches, butterflies. A miracle of urban greenery.
tips: Tucked away off Stacey Street — easily missed.

name: Kyoto Garden Holland Park
description: A Japanese garden gifted by Kyoto in 1991 — koi carp, maple trees, a tiered waterfall, resident peacocks.
tips: Quietest on weekday mornings.

name: Barbican Conservatory
description: London's second-largest conservatory — 2,000 tropical plants inside the Brutalist Barbican Centre, open Sundays only.
tips: Typically Sundays/bank holidays only. Free.

name: Hill Garden and Pergola
description: Lord Leverhulme's Edwardian Hampstead pergola and garden — an Italianate ruin of vines on the edge of Hampstead Heath.
tips: Free. Accessed via Jack Straw's Castle pub.

name: Chelsea Physic Garden
description: London's oldest botanic garden (1673) — 5,000+ medicinal, rare and edible plants behind walled-in Chelsea streets.
tips: Closed winters (Nov-Feb).

name: Garden Museum
description: A Lambeth church turned garden-and-gardening museum — the Tradescant knot garden outside, art exhibitions inside.
tips: Café in the former churchyard is lovely.

name: Crossrail Place Roof Garden
description: A lattice-domed rooftop park suspended above Canary Wharf Crossrail — a divided 'garden of hemispheres' of different plantings.
tips: Free. Access from Canary Wharf Crossrail station.

name: God's House Tower
description: A medieval gate-tower on the old Southampton city walls — survives intact in a part of London's history most don't know.
tips: 1.5h train from Waterloo.

name: John Betjeman Statue, St Pancras
description: A bronze of the poet looking up at the train shed he saved — Betjeman's campaign saved St Pancras from demolition in the 1960s.
tips: Near Platform 1. Below the roof he celebrated.

name: Paddington Bear Statue
description: A life-size bronze of Paddington, the little-bear-from-darkest-Peru — on Platform 1 at Paddington Station, holding his suitcase.
tips: Free. Near the 'Platform 1 help point'.

name: Peter Pan Statue
description: The 1912 Peter Pan statue by George Frampton in Kensington Gardens — installed in secret overnight by JM Barrie.
tips: Kids can climb on parts of the plinth.

name: Sphinxes at Cleopatra's Needle
description: Two bronze sphinxes flanking Cleopatra's Needle — look closely for WWI shrapnel scars and bomb damage from the first air raid on London.
tips: Date of 4 September 1917 bombing is marked.

name: Isaac Newton Statue at British Library
description: Eduardo Paolozzi's 1995 bronze of Newton, reworked from William Blake's famous engraving — peaceful piazza setting.
tips: Free. Courtyard of the British Library.

name: Battle of Britain Memorial
description: Paul Day's bronze London memorial (2005) to the Few — on the Embankment, with life-size figures of WWII airmen.
tips: Free. Lit dramatically at night.

name: Memorial to the Sinking of the SS Mendi
description: A moving memorial to the 646 South African Labour Corps soldiers who drowned in 1917 — at Hollybrook Cemetery, Southampton.
tips: Check Southwark Council website for current location.

name: Conscientious Objectors' Stone, Tavistock Square
description: A modest stone commemorating those who refused to fight — the only memorial of its kind in the UK.
tips: Also: Gandhi statue in the same square.

name: 7/7 Bombing Memorial, Hyde Park
description: 52 stainless-steel pillars, one for each victim of the 2005 London bombings — a restrained, moving installation in Hyde Park.
tips: Near Lovers' Walk. Bronze plaque lists all 52 names.

name: Sarah Parker Remond Memorial
description: A tiny but moving plaque to the abolitionist — outside Sir John Soane's Museum in Lincoln's Inn Fields.
tips: Hyde Park south side.

name: Holborn Ghost Sign
description: A faded painted ad for 'Criterion' brand whisky on a Holborn wall — one of dozens of 'ghost signs' across London.
tips: London Ghost Signs blog catalogues dozens more.

name: Spitalfields Ghost Signs
description: Fournier Street's fading Victorian painted advertisements — for tailors, coffee-rooms, and forgotten brands. A living archaeology of London commerce.
tips: Self-guided walk on London Ghost Signs blog.

name: Shoreditch Ghost Signs
description: Redchurch Street, Cheshire Street, and Bethnal Green Road — a concentration of the best-preserved Victorian painted signage in London.
tips: Combine with the Brick Lane street-art walk.

name: Leather Lane Ghost Sign
description: An enormous fading 'STEPHENS INK' painted sign on Leather Lane — a relic of the leading brand of blue-ink bottles.
tips: Free, visible anytime.

name: St Pancras Renaissance Hotel Interior
description: George Gilbert Scott's 1868 neo-Gothic masterpiece — walk into the lobby to see the Grand Staircase for free.
tips: Buy a drink at the Booking Office Bar for interior access.

name: Alexandra Road Estate
description: Neave Brown's 1978 low-rise Brutalist terraced estate — Grade II*-listed, a hidden architectural masterpiece.
tips: Respect residents — no interior access.

name: Trellick Tower
description: Ernő Goldfinger's 1972 Brutalist-residential tower — listed Grade II*, famously used as a villain lair by Ian Fleming.
tips: Free to view exterior. Combine with Portobello Road Market.

name: Strawberry Hill House
description: Horace Walpole's 1749 'little Gothic castle' — the first Gothic Revival house, whimsically turreted with fan-vaults.
tips: Closed Mon-Tue. Strawberry Hill station adjacent.

name: Red House (William Morris)
description: William Morris's 1860 home by Philip Webb — the founding building of the Arts and Crafts movement, with Burne-Jones murals inside.
tips: National Trust. Book guided tour to see murals.

name: 2 Willow Road (Goldfinger House)
description: Modernist architect Ernő Goldfinger's 1939 Hampstead home — where Ian Fleming's villain got his name, preserved as a living Modernist museum.
tips: National Trust. Small tours only — book ahead.

name: The Fan Museum
description: The world's only museum dedicated to hand-fans — 4,000 fans from 11th century to now, inside a restored Georgian Greenwich house.
tips: Afternoon tea in the Orangery £30 weekends.

name: Clockmakers' Museum
description: The world's oldest clock collection — 600 timepieces, free, inside the Guildhall Art Gallery.
tips: Free. Combine with the Roman amphitheatre remains in the basement.

name: Hunterian Museum
description: The Royal College of Surgeons' anatomical collection — thousands of preserved body parts from John Hunter's 18th-century collection.
address: Royal College of Surgeons, 38-43 Lincoln's Inn Fields, London WC2A 3PE
tips: Free but book ahead. Not for the squeamish.

name: Sir John Soane's Museum
description: The architect's eccentric 1837 house — crammed with thousands of architectural fragments, paintings, and sarcophagi.
tips: Free. Candle-lit tours first Tuesday of the month.

name: Cartoon Museum
description: The UK's only museum dedicated to British cartoon and comics — Hogarth to Beano, all on Wells Street.
tips: Walking tours around Soho available.

name: Petrie Museum
description: UCL's Egyptian archaeology museum — 80,000 artefacts in a tiny single room. One of the world's greatest Egyptian collections.
tips: Free. Torches provided — the room is dimly lit.

name: Grant Museum of Zoology
description: UCL's zoology museum — 68,000 specimens, a micro-skulls case of hundreds of tiny animal heads, and a quagga skeleton (extinct since 1883).
address: Rockefeller Building, 21 University St, London WC1E 6DE
tips: Free. Closed Sundays.

name: Wellcome Collection
description: A free library and museum of 'medicine, life and art' — Napoleon's toothbrush, Darwin's walking stick, Freud's couch, contemporary art.
tips: Free. Reading Room upstairs is a gorgeous public library.

name: Florence Nightingale Museum
description: A tiny museum inside St Thomas' Hospital — preserves the story of the founder of modern nursing.
address: St Thomas' Hospital, 2 Lambeth Palace Rd, London SE1 7EW
tips: Combine with a Thames-side walk past Parliament.

name: Old Operating Theatre
description: The only surviving 19th-century operating theatre in the UK — a wooden amphitheatre above a chapel, used before anaesthesia.
tips: Climb 52 steps up a spiral staircase — not for the mobility-impaired.

name: Magic Circle Museum
description: The world's most prestigious society of magicians opens its HQ for limited tours — props from Tommy Cooper, Houdini, Paul Daniels.
tips: Some tours include live magic.

name: Museum of Brands
description: 12,000 items of British consumer culture since the Victorian era — soap to cereal boxes, arranged chronologically.
tips: Combine with Portobello Road Market.

name: Vagina Museum
description: The world's first bricks-and-mortar museum dedicated to gynaecological anatomy — facts, myths, humour.
tips: Free, donations welcome.

name: Cinema Museum
description: A vast collection of cinema memorabilia housed in the old Lambeth workhouse where Charlie Chaplin briefly lived as a child.
tips: Access by guided tour only.

name: Ragged School Museum
description: The largest 'ragged school' Dr Barnardo opened for London's poor — a preserved Victorian classroom, kitchen, and schoolmaster's bedroom.
tips: Free. Monthly 'Victorian lesson' days for kids.

name: Twinings Shop & Museum
description: The world's oldest tea shop (1706) — a tiny museum at the back tells the family's 300-year history, Royal Warrants on display.
tips: Free. Tasting bar at the front.

name: London Silver Vaults
description: Underground vaults (1885) with 30 silver specialist dealers — the world's largest retail antique silver collection.
tips: Closed Sundays. Free to wander.

name: The Foundling Museum
description: The story of London's first children's home — art donated by Hogarth and Handel, tokens left by destitute mothers in the 1700s.
tips: Haunting and beautiful.

name: Bank of England Museum
description: Free museum inside the Bank of England — see a real £1m note, hold a gold bar, trace the story of British currency.
tips: Free. Mon-Fri only. Photo ID required to enter.

name: Faraday Museum at the Royal Institution
description: Michael Faraday's preserved basement laboratory — where he discovered electromagnetism. Free, with science demonstrations in the historic theatre upstairs.
tips: Free. Tuesday 1pm demonstrations are free.

name: Benjamin Franklin House
description: The only surviving home of Benjamin Franklin — he lived here 1757-1775. Immersive 'Historical Experience' tour.
tips: Tour books up — reserve ahead.

name: Dr Johnson's House
description: Home of Samuel Johnson while compiling his landmark 1755 Dictionary — a Queen Anne townhouse hidden off Fleet Street.
tips: Statue of his cat Hodge outside.

name: Handel & Hendrix in London
description: Two musicians 200 years apart lived in adjoining Mayfair houses — Handel upstairs, Hendrix next door. Extraordinary coincidence turned museum.
tips: Hendrix's flat preserved as in 1969.

name: Freud Museum
description: Sigmund Freud's final home — his couch, study, collection of antiquities all preserved as in 1938.
tips: Closed Mon-Tue.

name: Keats House
description: The Hampstead house where John Keats wrote 'Ode to a Nightingale' in 1819 — Regency atmosphere, garden, preserved manuscripts.
tips: Free admission last Sunday of each month.

name: Charles Dickens Museum
description: The only Dickens home open to the public — where he wrote 'Oliver Twist' and 'Nicholas Nickleby' in 1837-1839.
tips: Combine with a walk along Dickens's favoured alleys.

name: Sherlock Holmes Museum
description: A Victorian townhouse re-created at 221b Baker Street — fully furnished as Conan Doyle described it.
tips: Queues weekend mornings.

name: Leadenhall Market Green Dragon
description: A painted dragon on the rear-end of Leadenhall Market's central arcade — near-invisible without looking up.
tips: Look up at the corners of the arcade.

name: Clerkenwell Well
description: The medieval 'clerk's well' that gave Clerkenwell its name — preserved behind a modern glass wall.
tips: Look through the window — free to view.

name: The Gherkin's Secret Pigeons
description: The Gherkin has a hidden ring of perches at its top — part of the architect's design to 'welcome birds'.
tips: Binoculars help.

name: Rolling Bridge, Paddington
description: Thomas Heatherwick's extraordinary curling footbridge — rolls into a figure-of-eight every Wed at noon and Fri at 2pm.
tips: Check Merchant Square website for current schedule.

name: The Blackfriar Interior
description: An Art Nouveau gilded pub near Blackfriars — mosaic friezes, bronze friars, marble counter. Free to step inside.
tips: Stand at the bar with a drink — study the mosaics.

name: Viaduct Tavern Newgate Cells
description: Below the Viaduct Tavern pub — original cells from the old Newgate Prison, tours free on request.
tips: Ask the bartender. Tours free with a drink.

name: St Pancras Ghost Platform
description: An out-of-use platform 0 at St Pancras — where the Eurostar trains once turned. Visible from platform 1.
tips: Free. Look from the upper-level walkway.

name: Platform 10.90 (Between Worlds)
description: Under the King's Cross mainline rail platforms — a network of brick arches now used as King's Cross's Waitrose and shops.
tips: Walk through Coal Drops Yard to see the arches.

name: Camden Catacombs
description: Victorian horse-tunnels beneath Camden Market — originally for the canal's horses, now partly accessible via Camden Lock guided tours.
tips: Currently not publicly accessible — check Camden Market tours.

name: Stratford's Hidden Jubilee Line Station
description: The hidden upper concourse of Stratford station — designed but rarely used, visible from above on the Jubilee Line stairs.
tips: Used only for overflow concerts at the Olympic Park.

name: Embassy Gardens Sky Pool
description: A transparent glass-bottomed swimming pool suspended 10 storeys between two buildings — for residents, but visible from below.
tips: Look from the park below. Residents only in-pool access.

name: Floating Pocket Park
description: A floating garden on Paddington Basin — plants on a barge, a quirky urban-regeneration piece.
tips: Check Merchant Square website for current status.

name: Crystal Palace Park Dinosaurs
description: The first dinosaur sculptures ever made (1854) — still in Crystal Palace Park, scientifically outdated, magnificently Victorian.
tips: Free. Owners dined inside an unfinished iguanodon in 1853.

name: The Line Sculpture Walk
description: A modern-art walk along the Greenwich Meridian, with sculptures by Anish Kapoor, Anthony Gormley, Damien Hirst en route.
tips: Download the Line app for self-guided tour.

name: Wilton's Music Hall
description: The world's oldest surviving Grand Music Hall (1858) — saved from demolition, beautifully un-restored, a must for any London visitor.
tips: The Mahogany Bar accepts walk-ins even without a show.

name: Wilton's Music Hall Mahogany Bar
description: The Mahogany Bar inside Wilton's — an 1850s public bar preserved almost exactly. Free to enter, period-accurate atmosphere.
tips: Drink by gas-lamp. Ideal pre-theatre stop.

name: The Grenadier (Haunted Pub)
description: A Belgravia mews pub — haunted by a lashed-to-death officer; ceiling is pinned with £20 notes in his memory.
tips: Bring cash for the ceiling tradition.

name: Marylebone Lane
description: One of London's oldest un-straightened streets — curving and narrow, lined with independent shops. Like walking in the 1600s.
tips: Free. The original course of the Tyburn river.

name: Cecil Court (Booksellers' Row)
description: A tiny Victorian passage off Charing Cross Road — 20 antiquarian booksellers. Reputed inspiration for Diagon Alley.
tips: Mozart lived at number 9 in 1764.

name: Neal's Yard
description: A tiny, colourful courtyard hidden off Covent Garden's Monmouth Street — cobalt-blue-and-yellow painted shops, cafes, and community feel.
tips: Monmouth Coffee just outside.

name: Shad Thames
description: The Victorian warehouse-iron-bridged street beside Butler's Wharf — dramatic, cinematic, largely unchanged since the 1880s.
tips: A David Lean film location.

name: Amen Court
description: A 17th-century cobbled courtyard behind St Paul's — home to canons, with a wall said to be haunted by a 'Black Dog'.
tips: Combine with St Paul's Cathedral.

name: Wine Office Court
description: The narrow alley off Fleet Street — leads to Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese, where Dickens, Dr Johnson, and Mark Twain drank.
tips: Walk through to the pub.

name: Passing Alley
description: A tiny Clerkenwell passage — 3 feet wide, linking St John's Path to St John Street. Named for its use as 'Pissing Alley' in medieval times.
tips: Free. Walk through to St John Street.

name: Lincoln's Inn Old Hall
description: 15th-century hall inside Lincoln's Inn — Dickens worked here as a boy; it appears in Bleak House.
tips: Chapel free midday Mon-Fri.

name: Middle Temple Hall
description: Where Shakespeare's 'Twelfth Night' had its first recorded performance (1602) — oak-beamed, table and benches from Elizabeth I's era.
tips: Free, limited hours. Gardens open weekday lunchtimes.

name: Banqueting House
description: Inigo Jones's 1622 royal palace room — the last surviving piece of Whitehall Palace. Charles I was executed from a window outside.
tips: Rubens ceiling panels are the masterpiece.

name: Queens House Greenwich
description: Inigo Jones's first classical building in England (1635) — a white Palladian villa, free to visit, with the Tulip Stair the highlight.
tips: Free. Famous Tulip Stair the first cantilevered spiral.

name: Whitechapel Bell Foundry Site
description: The former site of the world's oldest bell foundry (1570) — cast Big Ben, the Liberty Bell. Building survives; foundry moved.
tips: Exterior visible — building now redeveloped.

name: Jewel Tower
description: One of only two surviving buildings of the medieval Palace of Westminster — a small 14th-century tower once holding royal treasure.
tips: English Heritage. Often missed beside Parliament.

name: Two Temple Place Mansion
description: A Victorian Neo-Gothic confection built for Waldorf Astor — free entry during winter-only exhibitions.
tips: Check if current exhibition is running.

name: Kenwood House
description: A 17th-century Hampstead Heath mansion with free-entry art collection — Vermeer, Rembrandt self-portrait, Gainsborough.
tips: Free. English Heritage. Lakeside walks after.

name: Eltham Palace Art Deco
description: Art Deco 1930s mansion built into the ruins of Henry VIII's palace — marble, veneer, glamour.
tips: English Heritage. Station at Mottingham.

name: Chiswick House
description: Lord Burlington's 1729 Palladian villa — one of Britain's first classical villas, with surrounding gardens of conservatories and sculpture.
tips: Grounds free; house ticketed.

name: Kew Palace
description: A small Dutch-gabled royal palace at Kew Gardens — George III's summer retreat and where he suffered his bouts of madness.
tips: Requires Kew Gardens ticket.

name: Osterley Park
description: A 16th-century country mansion remodelled by Robert Adam — one of the most complete Georgian interiors in Britain.
tips: National Trust. Piccadilly Line to Osterley.

name: Syon House
description: Home of the Dukes of Northumberland since 1594 — Robert Adam interiors, Capability Brown gardens, a 200-acre park.
tips: Closed in winter.

name: Capel Manor Gardens
description: A 30-acre historic estate — gardens in different historical styles, walled gardens, a maze.
tips: Combine with Myddelton House Gardens nearby.

name: Myddelton House Gardens
description: Plantsman E.A. Bowles's late-Victorian garden — rare plants, terraced lawns, Enfield-edge quirkiness.
tips: LVL volunteers lead tours.

name: Walthamstow Wetlands
description: Europe's largest urban wetland — 211 hectares of reservoirs, reedbeds, and a Victorian pumping station-turned-café.
tips: Free. Engine House has a café.

name: RSPB Rainham Marshes
description: 870 acres of reedbeds and wetlands on the Thames estuary — rare bitterns, water voles, architect-designed visitor centre.
address: New Tank Hill Rd, Rainham RM13 9BG
tips: Nearest Rainham station.

name: Ruislip Lido
description: A 60-acre reservoir turned beach, with a miniature steam railway and woodland walks — suburban surprise.
tips: Free parking. Miniature railway weekends only.

name: Thames Barrier Learning Centre
description: The enormous 1980s flood barrier — walk to it, see the silver hoods up close, and learn how it protects London.
tips: Test days (when gates raised) quarterly — witnessing it is thrilling.

name: Billingsgate Market
description: The UK's biggest inland fish market — 2am-8am Tuesday to Saturday, open to the public for a pre-dawn adventure.
tips: Free entry for public after 6am.

name: Smithfield Market at Dawn
description: The 800-year-old meat market, operating nightly — a sprawling Victorian iron-and-glass structure, at 3am-7am.
tips: Best before 7am. Closing permanently 2027.

name: New Covent Garden Market
description: London's wholesale flower-and-produce market since 1974 — in a vast Nine Elms warehouse, open 4am-10am.
address: New Covent Garden Market, London SW8 5EE
tips: Public access to flower market from 6am.

name: Columbia Road Flower Market (Sunday)
description: A Victorian East End street turned weekly flower market — Sundays 8am-3pm, a riot of blooms, chants, and street-food stalls.
tips: Arrive 9am to beat crowds. Best flowers sold at start.

name: Salter's Hall Garden
description: A tiny Livery hall garden in the City — free to visit on selected days, a peaceful retreat off Bread Street.
tips: Check Livery Hall open-days list.

name: Drapers' Hall Garden
description: A hidden garden at Drapers' Hall in the City — open only for tours and Open House events.
tips: Open House London weekend only.

name: Open House London Weekend
description: Every September, hundreds of London buildings open their doors for free — from City skyscrapers to private homes.
tips: Check Open House website in August for sign-up.

name: London Lost Rivers Tour
description: Self-guided walks following the paths of London's buried rivers — Fleet, Westbourne, Tyburn, Effra. The Fleet's course is a classic 2-hour walk.
tips: Download the 'Lost Rivers' free walking guide.

name: Oxo Tower Viewing Gallery
description: A free-entry viewing terrace on the 8th floor of Oxo Tower Wharf — Thames and City views without paying for a drink.
address: Oxo Tower Wharf, Bargehouse St, London SE1 9PH
tips: Free. Lift to the 8th floor.

name: The Garden at 120
description: A rooftop garden on the 15th floor of 120 Fenchurch Street — free, with panoramic City views and wisteria walks.
tips: Free, no booking. Weekdays 10-6:30pm.

name: Horizon 22
description: London's highest free viewing gallery — 58th floor of 22 Bishopsgate, 360° views of the city.
tips: Free but book ahead — releases 2 weeks in advance.

name: Tate Modern Level 10 Viewing
description: Free-entry 360° viewing level at the top of Tate Modern's Blavatnik Building.
tips: Free. Sunset over St Paul's is spectacular.

name: Sky Garden at Sky Pod Bar
description: Free access to Sky Garden — London's only free multi-storey viewing platform with tropical plants and Thames views.
tips: Free but book ahead.

name: The Monument Climb
description: Wren's 311-step 1677 spiral column — commemorating the Great Fire, with an astonishing head-spinning view.
tips: Receive certificate at the bottom.

name: St Paul's Whispering Gallery
description: 259 steps up inside St Paul's dome — whisper at the wall, and a listener 30m away hears every word.
tips: Continue to Stone Gallery (378 steps) and Golden Gallery (528 steps).

name: 40 Floral Street Roof Garden
description: A rooftop garden atop Comyn Ching's 1978 Floral Street building — open occasionally, a hidden Covent Garden secret.
tips: Rarely open — check Open House London.

name: SILO Zero-Waste Restaurant
description: Hackney Wick's world-first zero-waste restaurant — architect-designed café/restaurant, no bins, everything-composted philosophy.
address: Queens Yard, White Post Ln, London E9 5EN
tips: Tasting menu only. Book weeks ahead.

name: Grove House Chiswick
description: A Regency-era villa hidden behind walls in Chiswick — one of London's best-preserved early 19th-century houses.
tips: Exterior only — private residence.

name: Tooting Bec Common Wild Swimming
description: A London spot where Hampstead Heath ponds are famous but Tooting Bec lido is a lesser-known free open-air paradise.
tips: 90m unheated — refreshing.

name: Highgate Cemetery East
description: The East side of Highgate Cemetery — less famous than the West but home to Karl Marx, George Eliot, and Douglas Adams.
tips: West side requires a guided tour.

name: Postal Museum Mail Rail
description: The Post Office Railway — a 100-year-old narrow-gauge line 20m below Mount Pleasant. Ride the trains.
tips: Book Mail Rail ride ahead.

name: Grand Union Canal Boat Trip
description: A 3-hour narrowboat cruise from Little Venice to Camden and back — lock operation, canal-side houses, a dozen bridges.
tips: London Waterbus is the classic operator.

name: Hammerton's Ferry Hampton
description: A hand-pulled foot ferry across the Thames between Ham House and Marble Hill — runs every half-hour in summer, one of London's oldest ferries.
tips: Cash only. Seasonal — Easter-October.

name: The Paddington Hackney Carriage
description: A tiny Paddington walkway with original 19th-century gas lamps and a carriage archway — unchanged since 1890.
tips: Best photographed at dusk.

name: Genesis Cinema Projection Room
description: A Mile End cinema since 1939 — the upstairs projection room preserves original 35mm reels; ask at the bar for a peek.
tips: Ask staff — usually accommodating.

name: Greenwich Foot Tunnel
description: A Victorian cast-iron-clad tunnel beneath the Thames — walk from Greenwich to Isle of Dogs, 370 metres below ground.
tips: Free. Open 24/7. Lifts mostly work.

name: Woolwich Foot Tunnel
description: Sister tunnel to Greenwich — a 504-metre subterranean walk beneath the Thames, built 1912, less-visited.
tips: Free. 24/7. Combine with the Thames Barrier.

name: Old Royal Naval College Painted Hall
description: Wren's 'Britain's Sistine Chapel' — a 40,000-sq-ft painted ceiling by James Thornhill, in the heart of Greenwich.
address: Old Royal Naval College, London SE10 9NN
tips: Torch app lets you see ceiling details.

name: Horniman Museum Anthropology
description: The Horniman's extraordinary Natural History Gallery — taxidermied walrus-overstuffed-in-Victorian-times, anthropology collection from across the world.
tips: Free. Gardens free.

name: Mayflower Pub Steps
description: The jetty at The Mayflower pub — reputedly where the Mayflower ship sailed for America. Original timber steps.
tips: Walk out on the jetty — free access.

name: Museum of London Docklands
description: Inside a Georgian sugar warehouse — the story of London's river, port, and docks. Free entry.
address: No 1 Warehouse, West India Quay, London E14 4AL
tips: 'Sailortown' immersive reconstruction is memorable.

name: Thames River Police Museum
description: The world's oldest police force (1798) — a tiny museum inside the still-working Wapping station.
tips: Book ahead — visits by appointment.

name: Whitechapel Library
description: The 'East End's university' — a Victorian library, training ground for Jack London, George Bernard Shaw, and Isaac Rosenberg.
tips: Now Whitechapel Idea Store — visit the rooftop garden.

name: Rivoli Ballroom
description: The last surviving 1950s ballroom in London — red velvet, glitterball, swing nights, Brockley.
tips: Swing dance nights Saturdays. Films too.

name: Abney Park Cemetery
description: A Nonconformist garden cemetery (1840) reclaimed as a nature reserve — a ruined Gothic chapel, overgrown, haunting.
address: 215 Stoke Newington High St, London N16 0LH
tips: One of the 'Magnificent Seven' cemeteries.

name: Brompton Cemetery Catacombs
description: Beatrix Potter stole character names from tombstones here — catacombs below the colonnades.
tips: Emmeline Pankhurst is buried here.

name: The Cake Shop at the London Review Bookshop
description: The tiny Bloomsbury café next door to the London Review Bookshop — some of London's best cakes (try the lamingtons).
tips: Opens 10am Mon-Sat.

name: Bloomberg Arcade Bucket of Flowers
description: A giant bronze bucket-of-flowers sculpture by Ron Arad at Bloomberg Arcade — a playful piece of public art in the City.
tips: Combine with the London Mithraeum below.

name: Queen Victoria's Crane
description: A rare 19th-century hand-cranked dockside crane in South Dock — working, last of its kind in London.
tips: Free. Walk along the Docklands.

name: Riff Raff at Rising Sun Collective
description: A Rotherhithe music venue hidden in a railway arch — gigs, cabaret, pop-up restaurants, community-programmed.
tips: Check Resident Advisor for current events.

name: Trafalgar Tavern Whitebait Suppers
description: Dickens's favourite riverside pub in Greenwich — still serves whitebait, in the same 1837 building.
tips: Check current whitebait menu availability.

name: De Gaulle's Office, Carlton Gardens
description: Number 4 Carlton Gardens — where Charles de Gaulle ran the Free French government-in-exile during WWII. Plaque outside.
tips: Free. Exterior only — still in use as an office.

name: The Old Curiosity Shop
description: A 16th-century timber-framed London shop — reputedly Dickens's inspiration for 'The Old Curiosity Shop'. Still trading.
tips: Currently a shoe boutique.

name: Buddhist Peace Pagoda, Battersea Park
description: A 1984 Japanese pagoda in Battersea Park — a peace offering by monks, one of only two in the UK.
tips: Free. Walk around for four different Buddha statues.

name: Diana Memorial Fountain
description: The Kathryn Gustafson granite ring in Hyde Park — a 2004 memorial you can wade through.
tips: Kids can paddle. Lifeguards in summer.

name: National Covid Memorial Wall
description: A 500m stretch of Embankment wall covered with 220,000 hand-painted red hearts — one for each UK COVID-19 death.
tips: Opposite Parliament. Volunteers still maintain.

name: Stevie Smith's Palmers Green
description: The suburban home of the cult poet Stevie Smith — blue plaque at 1 Avondale Road.
tips: Exterior only — walk through Grovelands Park.

name: The Sloane Square Fountain
description: Sloane Square's 1953 Coronation fountain — surrounded by Chelsea's shopping streets, a classic London gathering point.
tips: Free. The Royal Court Theatre opposite.

name: Kensington Roof Gardens
description: A 1938 1.5-acre rooftop garden above Derry and Toms department store — historically public but currently closed pending redevelopment.
tips: Currently closed. Check website for reopening news.

name: St Stephen Walbrook
description: Wren's favourite of his churches — a perfect-proportions domed interior that prototyped St Paul's.
tips: Henry Moore stone altar divides visitors.

name: St Benet Paul's Wharf
description: Wren's Welsh Metropolitan Church (1685) — unmodified since the 17th century, services in Welsh.
tips: Open Mon-Thu 1-3pm.

name: St James Garlickhythe
description: Wren's City church nicknamed 'Wren's Lantern' for its many windows — rebuilt from Blitz damage, spectacular white-and-gold interior.
tips: Open Mon-Fri lunchtimes.
